Every KYC decision is a product decision.

In our Tech Talk, Laurence Davies, Head of Engineering at Spritz Finance, explains why KYC is a system that's constantly being refined as a platform grows.

Every change to an onboarding flow shapes who makes it into a product. Add too much friction, and legitimate users drop off. Remove too much, and bad actors find a way in.

As products evolve, those tradeoffs become even more complex. New features, new user segments, and new fraud vectors constantly shift the balance between security and user experience.

posts.content:
Stablecoin payment volume is accelerating, and that means compliance needs to evolve just as quickly.

At an ACAMS event on Monday, Brian Frankel, our BSA/AML Officer and Head of Payments Compliance, joined Thomas A.(TRM Labs), Peter Piatetsky (Castellum.AI), and Tiffany Patrick CSPO MBA CAMS CBP (Citi) to discuss how financial institutions can navigate the intersection of sanctions, digital assets, and modern payments.

A few insights the panel shared:

- Real-time screening and network-level due diligence are becoming the new baseline for managing sanctions risk
- Stablecoin payments require compliance controls at the point of execution, not just during onboarding, because transactions are fast and irreversible
- Compliance teams should watch for evolving sanctions evasion typologies, including mixer usage, cross-chain bridges, rapid fund cycling, and non-compliant exchanges

Thank you to the ACAMS Central Florida Chapter for hosting an engaging discussion and to the panelists for sharing their perspectives on the future of payments compliance.

The gap between what's possible and what's intuitive is where payment friction lives.

In our Tech Talk with Laurence Davies, Head of Engineering at Spritz Finance, he shared how the team experienced this firsthand. Their initial on-ramp relied on customers sending ACH credits to fund virtual accounts, which was a technically sound approach that revealed an unexpected insight: many users simply weren't familiar with initiating an ACH credit from their bank.

Adding ACH debits gave customers a funding experience they already understood to reduce friction while preserving the benefits of account-to-account payments.

If you're building a payments product, Modern Treasury's Payments API lets you offer ACH credits and ACH debits alongside named U.S. accounts, so customers can choose the funding method that works best for them.

How can we create faster feedback loops for developers and AI agents?

For years, we optimized our cloud Continuous Integration (CI) runs by improving caching, upgrading hardware, and streamlining pipelines. But even with those gains, feedback still arrived too late to keep developers and agents in flow.

In our latest journal, Harsh D., our Software Engineer, shares how we accelerated feedback loops by bringing CI back to developer machines and what we learned along the way:

- Reduced context switching by delivering feedback while developers are still working on a change
- Enabled AI agents to iterate against nearly every CI check locally
- Unified local and cloud workflows with a shared bin/ci command introduced by Rails 8.1
- Improved developer and agent workflows through a consistent development environment
- Shortened feedback-loop latency by eliminating cloud infrastructure overhead

The result: faster iteration, fewer interruptions, and more time spent building instead of waiting.

Read the full breakdown here: https://lnkd.in/gy5vwRyn

posts.content:
For seven years, Modern Treasury refused to touch your money.

It was the software between you and your bank.

Then Matt Marcus became CEO. Within eight months, it bought a stablecoin company and became a payment provider itself.

Meet Matt Marcus, Co-Founder and CEO of Modern Treasury. He co-founded the company in 2018, ran product for seven years, and took over as CEO in July 2025. The infrastructure he helped build has moved more than $400 billion for companies like Gusto, Navan, Procore, and Anchorage Digital.

The origin was unglamorous. At mortgage marketplace LendingHome, Marcus built the payment operations system. Volume grew from hundreds of payments a month to tens of thousands. The software could send the money. It could not explain it. Finance was still reconciling against bank statements by hand.

With co-founders Dimitri Dadiomov and Sam A., the 2018 thesis was simple: if payments start in software, software should monitor and reconcile them too.

That held for seven years. Modern Treasury connected to your bank and stayed out of the flow of funds.

Then the market moved:

➡️ July 2025: Marcus becomes CEO. Dadiomov moves to President

➡️ October 2025: Acquires Beam, a stablecoin on- and off-ramp platform founded by Visa's former crypto lead Dan Mottice

➡️ December 2025: Partners with Paxos, joins the Global Dollar Network

➡️ February 2026: Launches Modern Treasury Payments. Accounts, ACH, wire, RTP, FedNow, push-to-card, and stablecoins behind one API

➡️ March 2026: Joins Mastercard's Crypto Partner Program and becomes a Solana Foundation payments infrastructure partner

The numbers:

📈 $400B+ in payments processed, with customers moving hundreds of billions annually

📈 $183M raised. $2B valuation at the Series C

His philosophy:

💡 "Founders kept buying the wrong thing: full bank accounts, sponsorship structures, compliance overhead, when all they really needed was to move money safely."

💡 "We were coming with the fiat DNA. And they had the stablecoin DNA."

💡 "The future belongs to platforms that are fluent in both fiat and stablecoins and can operate responsibly across them."

What's next?

The stablecoin story is no longer about the coin. It is about the layer deciding which rail a payment uses. A treasury team does not want a crypto strategy. It wants a payout to land Sunday night, reconciled by Monday, and does not care whether that ran on FedNow or USDC.

Modern Treasury's bet is that nearly a decade of bank integrations and a ledger under every transaction beats any crypto-native platform at being that layer. 

The strongest stablecoin companies of 2030 may be the ones that never called themselves stablecoin companies.

Matt Marcus is testing that theory with a company that spent seven years avoiding the flow of funds entirely.

posts.content:
who is building the layer between tokenized deposits and stablecoins?

most of the talk on this topic pits one against the other. imo, the right framing is how will the two coexist?

a tokenized deposit is a digital representation of commercial bank money. it remains a liability of a specific bank and operates within that bank’s regulatory, liquidity, and risk perimeter. on the other hand, a stablecoin is an obligation of a separate issuer, backed by a pool of reserve assets, that’s generally designed to circulate beyond a single FI.

moving between them is therefore not simply a matter of transferring a token from one chain to another because they aren’t representing the same dollar. orchestration between the two requires substituting one regulated liability for another, and that needs several things to happen: the tokenized deposit balance must be transferred or redeemed on the bank’s ledger
stablecoins must be minted, redeemed, or sourced from available liquidity
compliance & eligibility controls must be evaluated. settlement risk must be managed across systems with different hours/FX/liquidity constraints/etc.

every movement must be reconciled to the appropriate system of record
today, three groups are converging on this problem: 
(1) stablecoin issuers are expanding the distribution and utility of their instruments, 
(2) banks are creating tokenized versions of commercial bank money, and 
(3) payment/settlement networks are connecting their members to new forms of digital money.

if the current trajectory holds, businesses will need to navigate a maze of banks, coins, wallets, chains, and settlement networks, so how will the industry create a layer between stables and another emerging form of dollars?

MT currently orchestrate fiat and stablecoin payments through a unified platform. that said, tokenized deposits have just begun to come up in industry discussions (though admittedly not yet with customers). regardless, this early signal just adds to the thesis that the future of tokenized money will be heterogeneous.

traditional bank deposits will remain systemically important for custodying cash and (sometimes) offering yield, credit, and treasury services. tokenized-deposit products from banks like JPM and Citi will support 24/7 payments and liquidity movement within (and between) regulated banking environments. stablecoins such as USDC, FIUSD, and SoFiUSD will be used for portable & programmable money movement across platforms and blockchain networks
ultimately, the puck is headed towards orchestration of ANY form of a dollar and we’re going to continue seeing that scope broaden, so we’re still in the early innings of what deep interoperability looks like

if any folks are building between stables and tokenized deposits, i’d love to connect and share more about what we’re seeing. it’s early, but it’s an important trend to watch
